# DATA ARCHITECTURE

*Summary: **Conversation Overview**

This was a wide-ranging, late-night deep research and strategy session with Phelipe Honesto, founder of Orange Sunshine Aviation (OSA), an ATP-rated First Officer at SkyWest Airlines building an AI-powered charter brokerage. The session covered aviation data intelligence strategy, book reviews, tool research, and strategic frameworks, building on months of prior work documented in OSA-Brain (Obsidian vault with 140+ processed conversations). Phelipe works across multiple Claude Code sessions using a CLAUDE.md system, pre-commit hooks, and a notification hook for session completion.

The session began with a comprehensive web research sweep on real estate voice AI reliability, validating that voice AI intake systems achieve 85-95% reliability for lead qualification — confirming OSA's plan to build a fully automated email pipeline first (99% reliable, already has Resend in Dumont's codebase) with voice as a Phase 3 addition. The core insight reached was that the entire charter deal flow — voice/form intake → operator sourcing → OSA-branded quote with Cost Anatomy → Mercury API payment → operator payout — can be fully automated with zero human involvement, responding in 15-45 minutes versus the industry's 15-hour average response time.

A major strategic thread developed around aviation data intelligence. Phelipe discovered that JETNET ($30-50K/year), WINGX (flight analytics), and ADS-B Exchange ($20M acquisition) can be substantially replicated using free public sources: FAA Aircraft Registry (daily CSV, free), ADS-B community forks (airplanes.live, adsb.fi — rebuilt after the JETNET acquisition out of community principle), UCC filings for loan-based price estimation (70-80% of aircraft purchases are financed, some filings show amounts), state corporation records, LinkedIn enrichment, AvBuyer/Controller listing scrapers, and OSA's own deal outcome data (which nobody else can replicate). The session produced a comprehensive aviation intelligence brief saved to /mnt/user-data/outputs/osa-aviation-intelligence-brief.md covering every dataset, build sequence, cost comparison, and accuracy progression. Honest accuracy assessment: OSA achieves ~68% of JETNET's blended accuracy on Day 1 with free automation, ~85% by Year 3 with one $55-65K remote analyst (former brokerage admin or FBO manager), and ~91% by Year 5 — while EXCEEDING JETNET on charter pricing intelligence from Day 1 because that data doesn't exist anywhere else.

The aircraft profile page concept emerged as a category-defining opportunity: publishing free, comprehensive aircraft intelligence pages (ownership, flight analytics, utilization rates, route patterns, estimated values, charter pricing) for all 170,000+ US-registered aircraft — comparable to what Zillow did for real estate, Carfax for vehicles, and Yahoo Finance for stocks. No competitor does this: FlightAware shows tracking only, Aviapages has operator-submitted data only, JETNET is behind a $50K paywall, and FAA registry is raw/ugly. Publishing ADS-B-derived analytics on public pages is legally sound (ADS-B is a public radio broadcast, FAA mandated it, and Zillow established the precedent for publishing analysis based on public records). The opt-out mechanism design was detailed: three tiers (remove live tracking only / remove value estimate / full page removal), verification requirement (email from company domain or legal documentation), and a "Claim Your Aircraft" feature that converts opt-out requests into operator acquisition opportunities.

Several tools were researched and classified for OSA's stack. TimesFM (Google's open-source time-series forecasting model, Apache 2.0) is a Year 2+ tool for predictive Charter Index pricing once 500+ deals accumulate. ClickHouse is the right database for ADS-B data at scale (billions of position records) and directly replaces WINGX's flight analytics capability via SQL queries on ingested ADS-B data. Fli (Python library for Google Flights data via MCP) enables real-time commercial vs. charter price comparisons on route pages, which is a unique competitive differentiator no other broker publishes. Aviapages was analyzed as the closest existing competitor — they proved demand exists for free charter tools but stopped at the directory layer with no AI, no payment processing, no real pricing intelligence, and no learning loop. Planespotters.net photos cannot be used commercially; the recommended approach is manufacturer press kit photos per aircraft type (free, high quality)*

Great, now I have everything I need.Here's what I found:

**Zach Wilson's repos and resources:**

- GitHub: github.com/eczachly — 30 repos, including the Data Engineering Handbook (34.8K stars)
- github.com/DataExpert-io/llm-driven-data-engineering — public repo covering LLM-driven data engineering concepts, including auto-generating SQL with Langchain
- Newsletter: blog.dataexpert.io (Substack) — 172K+ subscribers, #98 in Technology

**His core framework (from his April 6 article):**

The progression is: Raw Data → Dimensional Modeling → OBT → **AI-native aggregations** (question-specific datasets). AI thrives at mapping "question" to "appropriate data set" — like "What has happened with churn recently?" mapping to "customer_churn_detail." He calls this the rise of the **context engineer** — data engineers who summarize and create data marts on top of OBT models, dramatically reducing token cost by processing context with traditional tools like Spark and BigQuery.

**Direct application to Dumont:** Your orchestrator should work the same way. Don't have the Quote Agent reason over raw operator databases. Pre-compute named contexts: `route_pricing_KTEB_midsize_30d`, `operator_reliability_score_priester`, `aircraft_availability_window_next_72h`. The agent picks the right one based on the intake question.

**Other authorities to steal from:**

1. **Meta Engineering (just published April 6)** — They built a swarm of 50+ specialized AI agents that read every file in their codebase and produced 59 concise context files, resulting in 40% fewer agent tool calls. Their rule: "compass, not encyclopedia" — keep context files to 25-35 lines, actionable navigation beats exhaustive documentation. Directly applicable to how you structure Dumont's knowledge base.

2. **Materialize (context engines)** — They argue context for AI agents is not raw data in a single table but composite "business objects" like a "customer profile" or "order summary" — assembled from multiple sources, kept current as sources change, served directly to agents. This is basically what your Quote Agent needs: a live "quote context object" assembled from operator data, route history, and aircraft availability.

3. **Weaviate (context engineering for agents)** — Their open-source Elysia framework uses a decision-tree architecture where the agent evaluates the environment, available tools, past actions, and future options before choosing what to do next — each node has global context awareness. Very similar to your orchestrator pattern.

**The meta-insight across all of these:** The entire industry is converging on the same principle you're already building toward — don't give agents raw data, give them pre-computed, question-specific context objects. Zach calls them "AI-native aggregations," Meta calls them "context files," Materialize calls them "live business objects." Same idea, different names. The founders who implement this win on cost, speed, and accuracy simultaneously.

# Dumont Context Engineering Upgrade — ContextFactory, Pre-Aggregated Objects, Token Metering

Read all files before changing anything. Do not break the existing pipeline. This is a data architecture upgrade, not a rewrite.

---

## Background

Every capability currently receives a structuredClone of the full DealContext. This means every stage gets everything — guardian passes, presentation data, lane history — regardless of what it actually needs. This upgrade fixes three problems:

1. Context bloat (agents get irrelevant data, waste tokens, risk confusion)
2. No pre-aggregated intelligence (every deal recomputes from raw history)
3. No token visibility (usage is unmetered, all calls reserve 4096 output tokens)

These objects also serve as the foundation for future payment infrastructure and financial products. Design accordingly — they are permanent, not throwaway.

---

## Move 1: ContextFactory

Create a `ContextFactory` module. The orchestrator calls `ContextFactory.build('sourcing', dealContext)` instead of cloning the full DealContext.

Each slice is a typed Zod schema containing only what that stage needs:

| Stage | Slice Name | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| Intake | IntakeContext | Raw message, client history (if returning), airport lookup result |
| Guardian | GuardianContext | Trip params, regulatory flags, last 3 guardian passes only |
| Estimate | EstimateContext | Trip params, RouteIntel, aircraft class, wind/weather if available |
| PriceWall | PriceWallContext | Trip summary, physics estimate, client budget signal |
| Sourcing | SourcingContext | Trip params, RouteIntel, OperatorProfiles (filtered by route), budget ceiling |
| Quote | QuoteContext | Trip, RouteIntel, selected OperatorProfile, budget, ghost positioning value |
| Present | PresentContext | Route, client name, final price options, trip summary |
| Respond | RespondContext | Route, client name, final price, detected intent — 5 fields max |

Rules:
- Pure TypeScript. No LLM calls.
- Each schema is strict — no optional catchall fields.
- Guardian passes older than the last 3 are trimmed before passing downstream.
- laneHistory is removed from DealContext after sourcing completes.

---

## Move 2: Pre-Aggregated Composite Objects

These objects start empty and accumulate from Deal 1. No mock data. They are updated via hooks in `buildDealRecord` on every deal close or interaction.

### RouteIntel
Cached per route + aircraft class. TTL: 24 hours with manual refresh.

```ts
{
  route: string,              // "KTEB-KMIA"
  aircraftClass: string,      // "midsize", "super_mid", etc.
  avgPrice30d: number,
  dealCount: number,
  demandTrend: "rising" | "falling" | "stable",
  topOperators: string[],     // top 3 by reliability score on this route
  seasonalFactor: number,     // multiplier, 1.0 = baseline
  avgMarginDelta: number,     // physics estimate vs actual quote spread
  lastUpdated: Date
}
```

Dumont uses this for quote pre-calculation. avgMarginDelta becomes the Operator Margin Index.

### OperatorProfile
Cached per operator. Updated on every interaction.

```ts
{
  name: string,
  homeBase: string,            // overnight-parking-inferred from ADS-B — powers ghost positioning calc
  certs: string[],
  fleet: string[],
  avgResponseTime: number,     // minutes
  reliabilityScore: number,    // 0-1, Bayesian with time decay
  pricingDelta: number,        // typical markup over physics cost
  paymentSpeed: number,        // avg days to process payment
  quoteToBookRate: number,
  cancelRate: number,
  dealCount: number,
  lastUpdated: Date
}
```

Dumont uses this for sourcing. homeBase is critical — without it, SourcingContext cannot determine positioning cost, which is the single biggest pricing error the physics engine needs to avoid.

### ClientProfile
Cached per client. Updated on every deal.

```ts
{
  name: string,
  email: string,
  dealHistory: { route: string, price: number, date: Date, outcome: string }[],
  avgPaymentTime: number,      // hours from invoice to payment
  totalSpend: number,
  tripFrequency: number,       // trips per year
  preferredAircraftClass: string,
  preferredRoutes: string[],
  lastUpdated: Date
}
```

Dumont uses this for personalization. totalSpend triggers advisory conversations at $400K+.

### ValidationLedger
One row per deal attempt — booked or lost. This is a first-class data object, not a separate spreadsheet.

```ts
{
  route: string,
  date: Date,
  leadTimeHours: number,
  rliAtQuote: "high" | "medium" | "low",
  dumontPhysicsEstimate: number,
  ghostPositioningValue: number | null,
  operatorQuotedPrice: number,
  osaClientPrice: number,
  realizedMarginPct: number,
  rfqsSent: number,
  quotesReceived: number,
  operatorResponseMinutes: number,
  clientDecisionMinutes: number | null,
  outcome: "booked" | "lost_price" | "lost_timing" | "lost_ghosted" | "lost_other",
  fleetResilienceUsed: boolean,
  tripCompleted: boolean | null,
  notes: string
}
```

A new ValidationLedger row is written by buildDealRecord on every deal close. This is the artifact shown to YC — 15-20 rows proving unit economics, quote velocity, and operator signal quality.

### Storage
All objects live in-memory stores (same pattern as dealStore). Update hooks fire inside the existing learning loop — extend buildDealRecord, do not replace it.

---

## Move 3: Token Metering

Modify `safeLlmCall` with the following:

1. **Capture usage.** Read `response.usage` from every Anthropic API call. Log `{ inputTokens, outputTokens, model, capability, dealId }` to deal metadata.

2. **Right-size output tokens.** Add an `expectedMaxOutput` parameter per call type:
   - Intake parse: 512
   - Guardian check: 512
   - Estimate calc: 256
   - Respond draft: 1024
   - All others: 1024

**Day 1 physics stack (no APIs, pure computation):**

- Crew: flat day rate per aircraft class. $1,800 light, $2,400 midsize, $3,200 heavy. Adjust from real quotes.

# SQLite Migration — Replace JSON File Stores with SQLite

Read all files before changing anything. The goal: swap the persistence layer from JSON files to SQLite while keeping every existing interface identical. No capability, orchestrator, or test signature changes.

## Why

JSON file stores work for <100 deals but block Layers 2-5:
- No querying (every lookup is a full array scan)
- No concurrent access (file locks)
- No schema evolution (no migrations)
- No relational integrity (operator referenced in deal but deleted from store)
- No audit trail (overwrites destroy history)

## How

### Step 1: Install better-sqlite3

`npm install better-sqlite3` + `npm install -D @types/better-sqlite3`

better-sqlite3 is synchronous (matches our current writeFileSync pattern), zero-config, single-file database. No async migration needed.

### Step 2: Create a Database singleton

`src/memory/database.ts`

- Opens `./data/dumont.db` (or path from env var)
- Runs migrations on startup (create tables if not exist)
- Exports `getDb()` function
- WAL mode enabled for read performance
- Foreign keys enabled

### Step 3: Define migrations

`src/memory/migrations.ts`

One migration per table. Run in order on startup. Track applied migrations in a `_migrations` table.

Tables (match existing Zod schemas exactly):

**deals** — mirrors DealRecord schema
**route_intel** — mirrors RouteIntel schema. Composite key: (route, aircraft_class)
**operator_profiles** — mirrors OperatorProfile schema. Key: name
**client_profiles** — mirrors ClientProfile schema. Key: email (with name as secondary lookup)
**validation_ledger** — mirrors ValidationLedgerEntry schema. Append-only, no updates, no deletes
**deal_events** — NEW. Append-only event log for audit trail:
```sql
CREATE TABLE deal_events (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  deal_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  stage TEXT NOT NULL,
  event_type TEXT NOT NULL,  -- 'stage_entered', 'guardian_pass', 'guardian_block', 'estimate_generated', 'pricewall_cleared', 'quote_received', 'deal_closed', 'deal_lost'
  payload TEXT,              -- JSON blob of stage-specific data
  created_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now')),
  schema_version INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1
);
CREATE INDEX idx_deal_events_deal_id ON deal_events(deal_id);
```

This is the audit trail the CTO review flagged. Every stage transition writes an event. Immutable. Powers the financial compliance layer later.

**Money fields:** Store all prices as INTEGER cents, not floating point. Add a `currency TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'USD'` column alongside every price field. This is the Layer 4 blocker the CTO review identified — fix it now at the schema level so you never have to migrate later.

### Step 4: Rewrite JsonFileStore<T> to SqliteStore<T>

The generic base class you just extracted makes this clean. Replace the internals:
- `loadArray()` → `SELECT * FROM table`
- `save()` → individual INSERT/UPDATE statements
- `getAll()` → `SELECT * FROM table`
- Keep the same public interface on every subclass

Each store class (RouteIntelStore, OperatorProfileStore, ClientProfileStore, ValidationLedgerStore) keeps its exact public API. Only the internals change from JSON read/write to SQL read/write.

### Step 5: Migrate DealStore

Same approach. DealStore currently uses JSON. Swap internals to SQLite. Keep `recordDeal()`, `getByRoute()`, `getByOperator()`, `findClientDeals()`, `getAll()` signatures identical.

### Step 6: Add deal ID generation

Replace whatever generates `ctx.id` with a globally unique, sortable ID. Use `ulid` package (`npm install ulid`). ULIDs are:
- Sortable by creation time (useful for event log ordering)
- Globally unique (safe for multi-process later)
- 26 characters (compact)

### Step 7: Add schema versioning

## Claude

Brief explanation of what this prompt does.Right now your data lives in JSON files — one per store. Every read loads the whole file, every write rewrites the whole file. That works for your first few deals but it's a dead end.

SQLite replaces all those JSON files with a single `dumont.db` database file. Same machine, no server, no cloud database to manage. better-sqlite3 is synchronous so your existing code patterns don't change — you're just swapping what's behind the store classes you already built.

The reason to do it now instead of later: **every deal you close before the migration is data you have to convert afterward.** If you start on SQLite, every deal from Day 1 is stored correctly — integer cents (not floating point dollars), globally unique IDs (not random strings), versioned schemas (so you can evolve without breaking old rows), and an immutable event log (every stage transition recorded forever).

That event log is the piece that doesn't exist yet. Right now when a deal moves through INTAKE → GUARDIAN → ESTIMATE → PRICEWALL → SOURCING → QUOTE → PRESENT, there's no permanent record of that sequence with timestamps. The pipeline runs, the final state gets saved, but the journey disappears. The event log captures every step. That's what payment processors and regulators will want to see, and it's what powers your own analytics on where deals stall or drop off.

The prompt is structured so Claude Code swaps the internals of your existing store classes without changing any public interfaces. Your 658 tests keep passing because nothing above the storage layer changes — only what happens inside `JsonFileStore<T>` (now `SqliteStore<T>`).

# Full Codebase Audit — Polish, Professionalism, Security

Before doing anything, map the entire project:

1. Run `find src/ -type f -name '*.ts' | head -80` to see all source files
2. Run `find tests/ -type f -name '*.ts' | head -40` to see all test files
3. Run `cat package.json` to see dependencies
4. Run `cat CLAUDE.md` to understand the project context
5. Run `cat tsconfig.json` to see TypeScript config
6. Run `git log --oneline -20` to see recent history
7. Run `tree src/ -L 3` to see folder structure
8. Read every file in src/ before making any judgments

Then audit across these 5 dimensions. Be brutally honest. Score each 1-10.

## 1. Code Polish

- Are file headers consistent (description, purpose)?
- Are naming conventions consistent (camelCase, snake_case boundaries)?
- Are there dead imports, unused variables, commented-out code?
- Are error messages clear and actionable?
- Is there consistent use of TypeScript strict mode features?
- Any `any` types that should be properly typed?
- Are magic strings/numbers extracted to constants?
- Is the code readable by someone who didn't write it?

## 2. Security

- SQL injection vectors (parameterized queries or string concatenation?)
- Are secrets/API keys hardcoded anywhere?
- Is user input validated before reaching the database?
- Are there path traversal risks in file operations?
- Is the LLM output treated as untrusted before being used in operations?
- Does the Anthropic API key handling follow best practices?
- Are there any eval(), Function(), or dynamic code execution patterns?
- Is the SQLite database file permission-safe?

## 3. Production Readiness

- Are all console.log calls appropriate or should some be proper logging?
- Is error handling consistent (try/catch, error propagation)?
- Are there any process.exit() calls that would crash in production?
- Is graceful shutdown handled (close SQLite connections)?
- Are environment variables validated on startup?
- Is there a health check endpoint or readiness signal?
- Are there any synchronous operations that would block the event loop at scale?

## 4. Test Quality

- Run `npm test` and report the results
- Are there any test files that test implementation details instead of behavior?
- Are edge cases covered (empty inputs, null values, boundary conditions)?
- Do tests use proper isolation (no shared state between tests)?
- Are test descriptions clear enough to understand what failed without reading the test?

## 5. Architecture Consistency

- Does every module follow the same patterns (exports, error handling, naming)?
- Are barrel exports (index.ts files) complete and consistent?
- Is the dependency graph clean (no circular imports)?
- Are Zod schemas used consistently for validation boundaries?
- Is the separation between orchestrator, capabilities, memory, and schemas clean?

## Output

For each dimension, produce:
- Score (1-10)
- Top 3 issues (with file:line references)
- Recommended fix for each issue
- Whether the fix is mechanical (Claude Code can do it) or requires a design decision

Then produce a summary table:

| Dimension | Score | Critical Issues | Mechanical Fixes | Design Decisions |
|-----------|-------|----------------|-----------------|-----------------|

End with: "Ship-ready?" — YES or NO with the single biggest blocker if NO.

# Polish + Security + Production Readiness Fixes

The full codebase audit found 14 mechanical fixes needed. Do all of them in one pass. Read each file before editing.

## Security (5 fixes)

1. **Webhook verification default to reject** — bland-ai.ts:149 and resend.ts:131. When no webhook secret is configured, reject the request and log a warning. Never default to accepting unverified webhooks.

2. **CORS restrict origins** — server/index.ts:16. Replace open cors() with an allowlist from ALLOWED_ORIGINS env var. Default to localhost:5174 (dashboard) in dev, reject all others in prod.

3. **Vapi auth required in prod** — server/routes/vapi-llm.ts:78-86. When VAPI_SECRET is unset AND NODE_ENV=production, reject requests. In dev, log a warning but allow.

4. **Escape LIKE metacharacters** — deal-store.ts:163-168. The `%${needle}%` pattern lets a client name containing % match all rows. Escape %, _, and \ in the needle before constructing the LIKE pattern.

5. **Escape template regex keys** — templates/render.ts:40-42. User-controlled keys go into new RegExp(). Escape special regex characters before constructing the pattern.

## Production Readiness (3 fixes)

6. **Graceful shutdown** — server/index.ts. Add SIGTERM and SIGINT handlers that call closeDb(), close the HTTP server, then process.exit(0). Log "Shutting down gracefully..."

7. **Express global error handler** — server/index.ts. Add an error-handling middleware (err, req, res, next) after all routes. Log the error, return 500 with { error: "Internal server error" }. Never expose stack traces.

8. **Env var validation at startup** — server/index.ts. Before app.listen(), check that ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set. If missing, log an error and exit. Check VAPI_SECRET and BLAND_AI_WEBHOOK_SECRET with warnings (not fatal) in dev.

## Code Polish (4 fixes)

9. **Type SQLite rows** — deal-store.ts:27, composite-stores.ts:50,119,188,274. Define typed interfaces (DealRow, RouteIntelRow, OperatorProfileRow, ClientProfileRow, ValidationLedgerRow) for SQLite rows. Replace `row: any` with the typed interface in every rowTo* function.

10. **Rename save_message** — message-store.ts:40. Rename to saveMessage. Update all callers.

11. **Fix double-cast** — transcript-processor.ts:144. Replace `0 as unknown as string` with the correct comparison (speaker === "0" or String(speaker) === "0").

12. **Complete capabilities barrel export** — capabilities/index.ts. Add missing exports for respond, sdr, draft-evaluator, transcript-processor.

## Architecture (2 fixes)

13. **Router returns patch, doesn't mutate** — router/message-router.ts:131-168. Instead of directly mutating DealContext, return a patch object that the orchestrator merges. This maintains the "capabilities return data, orchestrator merges" invariant.

14. **Regression stage type safety** — orchestrator/stage-transitions.ts:181. The string "regression:presented→estimated" bypasses DealStage enum validation. Either add a regressionHistory string[] field to DealContext, or use a proper typed regression record instead of stuffing a non-enum string into the stage field.

- 656 tests must still pass after all fixes
- 0 type errors
- No interface changes to existing capabilities
- Security fixes should fail closed (reject by default, not accept by default)

The Five Real-World Cost Prevention Fixes
1. Anthropic Credit Drain via Unauthenticated Endpoint:
   * The Fix: Added an authentication middleware to `src/server/routes/conversation.ts` that enforces a Bearer token check against `DUMONT_API_KEY` or `VAPI_SECRET` before allowing requests to the LLM-triggering endpoint. Furthermore, the `guardian.ts` checks were updated to flag any margin exceeding 50% as a `critical` failure, completely halting the pipeline before a quote can be presented to a client.
3. Database Corruption via Partial Writes:
   * The Fix: The `recordDeal` function in `src/memory/learning-loop.ts` was entirely rewritten to execute within a single synchronous SQLite transaction (`db.transaction(() => { ... })`). This ensures that the primary deal record and all aggregated composite objects (RouteIntel, OperatorProfile, ClientProfile, ValidationLedger) are committed atomically. If any part of the process fails, the entire transaction rolls back, preventing orphaned records.
4. Prompt Injection Bypassing Guardian Safety Checks:

This function strips common prompt injection patterns (e.g., "ignore previous instructions," role impersonations like "system:", markdown fences, and XML-style tags) before the raw text is passed to the LLM parser as a fallback. While not impenetrable, it acts as a crucial layer of defense-in-depth.
5. Fintech Parsing Errors due to JSON Stringification:
   * The Fix: The `updateClientProfile` function in `src/memory/learning-loop.ts` was corrected to convert the floating-point `r.osaPrice` into integer cents (`Math.round((r.osaPrice ?? 0) * 100)`) before storing it within the `dealHistory` JSON object. # Final Pre-Launch Fixes: Guardian warnings, webhook idempotency, quote sanity check, Vapi-only cleanup

Read all files before editing. 656 tests must still pass.

## Fix 1: Guardian warnings halt pipeline before presentation

In src/orchestrator/index.ts, the pipeline only halts on "blocked" status. Warnings pass through silently — meaning an underpriced quote or uncertified operator reaches the client automatically.

Fix: After the final Guardian check (checksAfterQuote), if ctx.guardian.currentStatus is "warning", do NOT advance to "presented". Instead:
- Set ctx.stage to "awaiting_review"
- Add "awaiting_review" to the DealStage enum in src/schemas/deal-context.ts
- Add valid transitions: quoted → awaiting_review, awaiting_review → presented, awaiting_review → failed
- Log the warning reasons in ctx.outcome.notes
- The pipeline returns a result with outcome "awaiting_review" — the deal is alive but paused for human approval
- Only "passed" status advances to presented automatically

This is the single most important safety mechanism in the system. No deal with Guardian warnings should ever reach a client without human eyes.

## Fix 2: Quote price sanity check between regex and LLM

In src/router/message-router.ts, the quoteExtractor LLM result is trusted absolutely with no comparison to the regex result. If the LLM extracts a catering fee ($2,000) instead of the flight cost ($38,000), the pipeline advances with the wrong price.

Fix: After the LLM returns a confirmed price, compare it to the regex price:
```typescript
if (confirmed) {
  const deviation = Math.abs(confirmed.quotedPrice - regexPrice) / regexPrice;
  if (deviation > 0.25) {
    return { 
      type: "flag_for_human", 
      reason: `Price mismatch: regex found $${regexPrice.toLocaleString()}, LLM found $${confirmed.quotedPrice.toLocaleString()} (${(deviation * 100).toFixed(0)}% deviation). Manual review required.`
    };
  }
  return { type: "advance_to_quoted", operatorPrice: confirmed.quotedPrice };
}
```

25% threshold. If regex says $38,000 and LLM says $2,000, that's a 94% deviation — flagged for human. If regex says $38,000 and LLM says $40,000 (catering included), that's 5% — accepted.

## Fix 3: Webhook idempotency

Webhook providers (Vapi, Resend) retry if they don't get a 200 within ~10 seconds. If an LLM call takes 15 seconds, the webhook retries and Dumont processes the same payload twice — duplicate deals, duplicate emails, duplicate LLM costs.

Fix: Add a simple deduplication layer. In every webhook/POST handler that triggers async work:
1. Extract a unique key from the payload (message ID, call ID, or hash the body)
2. Check a `processed_webhooks` Set (or SQLite table for persistence)
3. If already seen, return 200 immediately with { status: "already_processed" }
4. If new, add to the set, return 200 immediately, THEN process async

For the SQLite approach, add migration 11:
```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS processed_webhooks (
  idempotency_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  processed_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
);
```

Add a cleanup that deletes entries older than 24 hours on the eviction interval.

The key insight: return 200 FIRST, process AFTER. Never await LLM calls inside a webhook handler's response path.

## Fix 4: Remove Bland AI — Vapi only

We only use Vapi for voice. Remove all Bland AI integration code:
- Delete src/integrations/bland-ai.ts entirely
- Delete src/channels/voice.ts if it's Bland-specific (check first — if it's shared with Vapi, keep it)
- Remove bland-ai imports from any barrel exports (src/integrations/index.ts, src/channels/index.ts)
- Remove BLAND_AI_WEBHOOK_SECRET from env var validation in server/index.ts
- Remove the Bland AI webhook verification test expectations
- Update CLAUDE.md to reflect Vapi-only voice
- Do NOT remove Vapi-related code (server/routes/vapi-llm.ts, server/dumont-brain.ts)
- Do NOT remove Resend (that's email, not voice)

If any test file imports from bland-ai.ts, update or remove those tests.

## Constraints
- 656+ tests must pass (some may be removed with Bland AI deletion)
- 0 type errors
- awaiting_review must be a proper stage with valid transitions
- Webhook handlers must return 200 before processing, never after
```

But if you ever do high-frequency aggregations across thousands of deals, those half-cents accumulate. The fix is using `Math.round((dollars + Number.EPSILON) * 100)` or a decimal library. Not urgent. Not blocking. Just know it exists.

# Architecture Polish — Prepare for API, New Agents, and Insight Analysis

Read every file in src/ before changing anything. Run the tests first. This is not a rewrite — it's a polish pass to make the codebase ready for rapid feature development by a solo founder using AI coding tools.

The goal: any new feature (API endpoint, agent capability, analysis query) should be addable by creating 1-2 files and touching 1-2 barrel exports. If the current architecture requires touching more than that, fix the architecture.

## Phase 1: Map the codebase

1. `tree src/ -L 3` — understand the structure
2. Read every barrel export (index.ts files) — are they complete?
3. Check for circular imports: `npx madge --circular src/`
4. Run `npm test` and `npx tsc --noEmit` — baseline

## Phase 2: Audit for extensibility

For each of these future features, trace what you'd need to touch today to add it. If the answer is more than 2 files + 1 barrel export, flag the architectural gap:

1. **New API endpoint** (e.g., GET /api/deals/:id) — is there a clean router pattern to follow?
2. **New agent capability** (e.g., a FollowUpEngine that triggers smart re-engagement) — can it follow the existing capability signature pattern?
3. **New composite object** (e.g., RouteHistory for time-series analysis) — can it plug into the SQLite store pattern without modifying existing stores?
4. **New insight query** (e.g., "what's our average margin on KTEB routes this month?") — can it query the database without importing store internals?
5. **New channel adapter** (e.g., WhatsApp) — can it follow the existing ChannelAdapter interface?

## Phase 3: Polish (do these fixes)

### 3A. Consistent file headers
Every file in src/ should have a JSDoc header block with:
- One-line description
- Which layer it belongs to (orchestrator | capability | memory | schema | server | router | channel | integration | util)
- No more than that — don't over-document

Files missing headers: add them. Files with stale headers: update them. Files with excessive headers: trim them.

### 3B. Consistent error handling
Audit every try/catch in src/. For each one:
- Is the catch specific enough? (catching Error vs catching unknown)
- Is the error logged with enough context to debug? (file, function, deal ID if available)
- Is the error swallowed silently? If so, is that intentional?

Standardize on this pattern:
```typescript
catch (err) {
  console.error(`[module:function] ${err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)}`);
  // rethrow, return fallback, or swallow — but never silently
}
```

### 3C. Extract a clean API router pattern
Look at server/routes/. If adding a new endpoint requires copying boilerplate (auth check, error handling, request validation), extract shared middleware:
- `authMiddleware` — checks Bearer token, returns 401
- `validateBody(schema)` — Zod-validates req.body, returns 400 with errors
- `asyncHandler(fn)` — wraps async route handlers with try/catch

This makes adding a new endpoint a 10-line file instead of a 40-line file.

### 3D. Capability registration pattern
Check if capabilities follow a consistent signature. If a new capability requires modifying the orchestrator switch/if chain, that's wrong. Consider:
- Do all capabilities have the same input/output shape?
- Can a new capability be added by creating a file and registering it?
- Is the capability → stage mapping explicit and discoverable?

If the orchestrator has hardcoded capability calls, document the pattern clearly in a comment block so the next capability follows the same shape. Don't over-abstract — just make the pattern obvious.

### 3E. Database query layer
Check if store methods are the only way to access SQLite, or if raw db.prepare() calls leak into capabilities/orchestrator. If they do, move them into the appropriate store. The rule: **capabilities never import from memory/ directly except through store interfaces.**

### 3F. Type exports
Check that every type used across module boundaries is exported from the nearest barrel. If a capability needs to import a type from deep inside another module (e.g., `../../schemas/deal-context.js`), that type should be re-exported from `schemas/index.ts`.

### 3G. Dead code removal
Find and remove:
- Unused exports (functions/types exported but never imported elsewhere)
- Commented-out code blocks
- TODO comments older than the SQLite migration (they're stale)
- Unused dependencies in package.json

### 3H. CLAUDE.md accuracy
Read CLAUDE.md end to end. Update:
- File tree (new files, deleted files)
- Test counts
- Provider stack (Vapi only, no Bland)
- Architecture description (SQLite, context factory, composite objects, deal events)
- Any stale references

## Phase 4: Verify

1. `npx tsc --noEmit` — 0 errors
2. `npm test` — all tests pass
3. `npx madge --circular src/` — 0 circular imports
4. Every barrel export is complete
5. Every file has a one-line header

## Output

Produce a summary:
- Files touched (with one-line description of change)

- Dead code removed
- Circular imports found and fixed (if any)
- Final test count and type check status

- Do not rename files or move directories
- Do not add dependencies unless absolutely necessary
- Tests must pass throughout — run them after every batch of changes
- This is a polish, not a refactor. If something works and is readable, leave it alone.

```
# Two final fixes — 5 minutes total

## 1. Webform input truncation
In src/channels/web-form.ts, wherever the raw form body is assembled, add:
const capped = body.slice(0, 2000);
Same pattern as intake.ts. Prevents 10MB paste attacks.

## 2. resumeDeal function
In src/orchestrator/index.ts, add:

export function resumeDeal(
  ctx: DealContext,
  action: "approve" | "reject",
  reason: string,
  eventLog?: DealEventLog,
): void {
  if (ctx.stage !== "awaiting_review") {
    throw new PipelineError(`Cannot resume deal in stage ${ctx.stage}`);
  }

  eventLog?.appendEvent(ctx.id, "awaiting_review", 
    action === "approve" ? "review_approved" : "review_rejected",
    { reason, reviewedBy: "founder" }
  );

  if (action === "approve") {
    advanceStage(ctx, "presented");
    ctx.outcome.notes = ctx.outcome.notes 
      ? `${ctx.outcome.notes}; Manual approval: ${reason}`
      : `Manual approval: ${reason}`;
  } else {
    advanceStage(ctx, "failed");
    ctx.outcome.notes = ctx.outcome.notes
      ? `${ctx.outcome.notes}; Rejected at review: ${reason}`
      : `Rejected at review: ${reason}`;
  }
}
```

# Mission Control v2 — Deal Operations Dashboard

Read the existing dashboard/ directory first. Understand the current component structure, routing, and data fetching patterns before changing anything.

## Design Authorities
- Linear: keyboard-first, information-dense, instant state transitions
- ForeFlight: layered aviation data in a single decision interface
- Bloomberg Terminal: monospaced numbers, maximum data density, dark theme

## Design Rules (Non-Negotiable)
1. Dark theme only. OSA palette: bg #0A0A0A, surface #141414, border #1E1E1E, text #E5E5E5, muted #666, accent #E74B1D (OSA Orange), success #22C55E, warning #EAB308, critical #EF4444
2. Monospaced font for ALL numbers, prices, percentages, deal IDs, ICAO codes, timestamps
3. No illustrations, no gradients, no rounded corners > 4px, no shadows, no animations except loading states
4. Every view must be keyboard-navigable. Arrow keys to move between deals, Enter to open, Escape to close, / to focus command bar
5. Information density: a deal card in the pipeline must show route, client, price, margin, stage, and time-in-stage WITHOUT expanding or clicking
6. Progressive disclosure: summary → detail → raw data. Each level is one click/keystroke deeper

## Tech Stack
- React (Vite, already set up in dashboard/)
- Tailwind CSS
- shadcn/ui for base components
- Recharts or Tremor for data visualization (KPIs, charts)
- React Router for views
- Fetch from Dumont API (GET /api/deals, etc — build the endpoints as needed)

## The Five Views

### VIEW 1: Pipeline (default view, keyboard shortcut: 1)

Layout: Left sidebar (30%) + Right detail panel (70%)

LEFT SIDEBAR — Deal List:
Each deal card shows in a single row or compact card:
- Client name (bold)
- Route: KTEB → KPBI (monospaced)
- Aircraft class + pax count
- OSA Price (monospaced, large): $30,978
- Stage indicator: colored pill matching stage
- Time in current stage: "12m" or "2h"
- Guardian status icon: ✓ (passed), ⚠ (warning — show in yellow), ✕ (blocked — show in red)
- If awaiting_review: show "REVIEW REQUIRED" badge in yellow, entire card has yellow left border

Sorting: Most urgent first (awaiting_review at top, then by time-in-stage descending)
Filtering: Keyboard-accessible filter chips for stage, guardian status

RIGHT PANEL — Deal Detail (when a deal is selected):

Three-column layout:

Column 1 — Trip & Client:
- Route: KTEB → KPBI with great circle distance
- Date, Pax, Aircraft Class/Type
- Client: Name, Contact, Type (new/repeat), Budget range
- Trip timeline: horizontal bar showing stage progression with timestamps

Column 2 — Pricing Engine:
- Physics Estimate: $26,000–$34,000
- Operator Quote: $28,500
- OSA Price: $30,978
- Margin: 8.0% (color-coded: green 8-15%, yellow 5-8%, red <5% or >20%)
- Ghost Positioning Value: $0 or "$3,200 saved" (if applicable)
- Estimate Delta: +5.4% (how accurate was the physics estimate)

Column 3 — Operator & Guardian:
- Selected Operator: name, base, aircraft, reliability score
- Operator response time
- Guardian Log: list of all checks with pass/warn/fail icons
  - Each check shows: check name, severity, message
  - Warnings highlighted in yellow
  - Critical failures in red

Action Bar (bottom of detail panel, above command bar):
- If stage === "awaiting_review": show [APPROVE] and [REJECT] buttons prominently
  - APPROVE calls resumeDeal(dealId, "approve", reason) — prompts for reason
  - REJECT calls resumeDeal(dealId, "reject", reason) — prompts for reason
- If stage === "quoted": show [PRESENT TO CLIENT] button
- If stage === "presented": show [CLOSE DEAL] and [MARK LOST] buttons
- Show [ENTER MANUAL QUOTE] button when in sourced/quoted stage

### VIEW 2: Inbox (keyboard shortcut: 2)

Current design is good. Enhance:
- Add channel icon (email, phone, web) next to each message
- Show deal ID linkage prominently — clicking it navigates to that deal in Pipeline view
- Add a "Reply" action that opens a draft compose inline
- Filter by: All, Unmatched, Needs Response

### VIEW 3: Calls (keyboard shortcut: 3)

Current "No active call" empty state is fine. When a call is active, show:
- Live transcript streaming in the center
- Deal context on the right (pulled from the linked deal)
- Detected entities highlighted in the transcript (prices, dates, aircraft)
- "Copilot suggestions" at the bottom — things Dumont thinks you should say based on the deal context

### VIEW 4: SDR (keyboard shortcut: 4)

Current kanban is good. Enhance:
- Add the "auto" badge explanation — tooltip: "Dumont auto-responded because this template has earned autonomy (10+ zero-edit approvals)"
- Add counts per column header (already there, keep it)
- Make cards clickable → opens the deal in Pipeline view
- Add qualification rate and auto-response rate as KPI badges at top

### VIEW 5: Intelligence (keyboard shortcut: 5 — NEW VIEW)

This is the data moat visualization. Two sections:

Section A — Validation Ledger (the YC artifact):
- Full table view of the validation_ledger SQLite table
- Columns: Route, Date, Lead Time, RLI, Physics Estimate, Ghost Value, Operator Quote, OSA Price, Margin%, RFQs Sent, Quotes Received, Operator Response (min), Client Decision (min), Outcome, Notes
- Color-code outcomes: booked=green, lost_price=red, lost_timing=yellow, lost_ghosted=gray
- Sort by date descending (most recent first)
- Export to CSV button (for YC pitch prep)
- Summary stats row at top: Total Deals, Win Rate, Avg Margin, Avg Response Time, Total Revenue

Section B — Learning Loop KPIs (below the ledger):
- 4 metric cards in a row:
  1. Deals: total / closed / conversion rate
  2. Revenue: total $ / avg deal size
  3. Avg Margin: % with trend arrow
  4. Estimate Accuracy: avg delta % (how close physics estimates are to actual quotes)
- Route performance chart: bar chart of top 10 routes by deal count
- Operator leaderboard: table of operators sorted by reliability score, showing deals, response time, conversion rate

### VIEW 6: Autonomy (keyboard shortcut: 6)

Current design is excellent. Keep it. Only add:
- Channel filter (show only email, only voice, etc)
- "Demote" button already exists — add "Force Promote" for testing (with confirmation dialog)

## Command Bar Enhancement

The command bar at the bottom is your primary interaction surface. Add these commands:

/review [approve|reject] [reason] — Resume a deal from awaiting_review
/quote [amount] — Manually enter an operator quote for the selected deal
/ledger — Switch to Intelligence view, scroll to Validation Ledger
/deal [id] — Jump to a specific deal in Pipeline view
/export — Export Validation Ledger to CSV and download

## API Endpoints Needed

Build these Express routes using the middleware pattern from src/server/middleware.ts:

GET /api/deals — returns all deals from DealStore (with pagination later)
GET /api/deals/:id — returns a single deal by ID
GET /api/deals/:id/events — returns deal events from DealEventLog
POST /api/deals/:id/review — { action: "approve"|"reject", reason: string } — calls resumeDeal
POST /api/deals/:id/quote — { operatorPrice: number } — manually enters a quote
GET /api/ledger — returns ValidationLedger entries
GET /api/ledger/export — returns CSV
GET /api/metrics — returns Learning Loop KPI summary
GET /api/operators — returns OperatorProfile summaries

All endpoints use authMiddleware. All use asyncHandler. All validate input with Zod via validateBody where applicable.

## Constraints
- Dashboard must work on 1440px+ screens (your MacBook). Mobile is not a priority.
- All data fetches use SWR or React Query for caching + auto-refresh (30 second polling)
- The dashboard reads from Dumont's SQLite database via API — it never imports from src/memory directly
- 628 backend tests must still pass — the API endpoints are additive
- Use the existing OSA color palette, not generic Tailwind colors

I have a detailed architecture prompt ready for my coding assistant. Before I run it, I want your input as a product designer and UX engineer who understands financial operations tools (Bloomberg, Linear, ForeFlight).

## What I need from you:

### 1. Critique the current screenshots
Look at each screenshot and tell me:
- What works and should be kept exactly as-is
- What's broken from a UX perspective (information hierarchy, wasted space, missing affordances)
- What's missing that a deal operator would need in the first 10 seconds of looking at the screen

### 2. The Intelligence View
I'm adding a new "Intelligence" tab that surfaces the ValidationLedger (my YC proof artifact) and the Learning Loop KPIs. Design this view:
- What metrics belong above the fold?
- How should the ValidationLedger table be structured for a solo founder who needs to spot patterns in 15-20 rows of deal data?
- What charts actually earn their screen real estate vs. what's vanity?
- How would you visualize the Ghost Positioning Spread, Operator Signal Ratio, and Route Liquidity Index?

### 3. The Deal Detail Panel
The right panel shows deal details when you click a deal in the pipeline. Currently it's a flat vertical list (Route, Client, Pricing, Operator sections stacked). For a $40,000 transaction, what information architecture would you use? Think about:
- What does the founder need to see FIRST to decide "is this deal healthy?"
- How should Guardian warnings surface without overwhelming the panel?
- Where does the "approve/reject" action go for awaiting_review deals?
- How would you show the pricing waterfall (Physics Estimate → Operator Quote → OSA Price → Margin)?

### 4. Missing Views
Based on the brain dump and moat documents, are there views I'm not building that I'll need within 90 days? Consider:
- The operator relationship layer (Priester's response times, conversion rates, pricing deltas over time)
- The client lifecycle (repeat client detection, total spend tracking, advisory triggers at $400K+)
- The financial operations layer (Mercury payment status, invoice tracking, float exposure per deal)

### 5. Interaction Design
The command bar is the primary interaction surface (like Linear's CMD+K or a terminal). Evaluate:
- Is a terminal-style command bar the right pattern for a solo founder managing 3-5 active deals?
- Should some actions be promoted to buttons/hotkeys instead of typed commands?
- What keyboard shortcuts would a power user expect? (Think Bloomberg terminal key bindings)

### 6. Design System Critique
Looking at the screenshots:
- Is the color coding consistent and meaningful? (Orange for OSA brand, green for success, red for critical, yellow for warning)
- Is the typography hierarchy clear? (What's a heading vs. a label vs. a value?)
- Is the information density appropriate or is there too much/too little?

Be specific. Reference the screenshots by number. Give me concrete changes, not abstract principles. I want to merge your feedback into the architecture prompt before I build.

## Claude

The user wants to add an AI chat interface to Mission Control where they can talk to Dumont directly - essentially Claude with the aviation domain knowledge, deal context, and intelligence layer built into the system prompt.Yes. And this is high leverage — you're not just adding a chat widget, you're building the interface where you'll eventually interact with Dumont as a co-pilot instead of clicking through UI panels.

**Day 1 version (build now):** A chat panel in Mission Control that sends your message to Claude via your existing `safeLlmCall`, with a system prompt that includes the current deal context, operator profiles, route intel, and ValidationLedger summary. You ask "what's the best operator for KTEB-KMIA midsize next Tuesday?" and it answers using your actual data.

**What it becomes later:** Your fine-tuned model that knows every deal you've ever closed, every operator's pricing behavior, every route's seasonal patterns. But that's at 500+ deals. Today it's Claude with a fat system prompt.

The architecture is one new view in the dashboard + one new API endpoint:

```
# Dumont Chat — AI Co-Pilot in Mission Control

## Backend: POST /api/chat

In src/server/routes/chat.ts:

- Accepts { message: string, dealId?: string }
- Builds a system prompt that includes:
  - If dealId provided: full DealContext for that deal (route, pricing, guardian status, operator)
  - Last 5 ValidationLedger entries (so Dumont knows recent deal patterns)
  - Top operator profiles (names, scores, response times)
  - Current pipeline summary (how many deals in each stage)
- Calls safeLlmCall with the system prompt + user message
- Streams the response back via SSE (server-sent events) for real-time typing feel
- Uses authMiddleware — no unauthenticated chat

The system prompt should start with:
"You are Dumont, the AI deal engine for Orange Sunshine Aviation. You are talking to Phelipe, the founder and pilot-in-command. You have access to the current deal pipeline, operator intelligence, and pricing data. Answer questions about deals, operators, routes, and pricing using the data provided. Be direct, use numbers, no filler."

## Frontend: ChatView component

- New tab in Mission Control: "Dumont" (keyboard shortcut: 7)
- Simple chat interface: message list + input field at bottom
- Messages stream in token-by-token (SSE)
- If a deal is selected in Pipeline when you switch to chat, that deal's context is automatically loaded
- Command bar: /chat [message] sends a message without switching tabs
- Monospaced font for any numbers/prices in responses
- Dark theme matching the rest of Mission Control

## Context injection (the intelligence layer)

Build a function buildChatContext(dealId?: string) in src/server/routes/chat.ts that assembles the system prompt from real data:

```typescript
function buildChatContext(dealId?: string): string {
  const parts: string[] = [];
  
  // Pipeline summary
  const deals = dealStore().getAll();
  const byStage = groupBy(deals, d => d.result);
  parts.push(`Pipeline: ${deals.length} total deals. ${JSON.stringify(byStage)}`);
  
  // If specific deal selected
  if (dealId) {
    const deal = deals.find(d => d.id === dealId);
    if (deal) parts.push(`Current deal: ${JSON.stringify(deal)}`);
  }
  
  // Recent ledger entries
  const ledger = validationLedger().getAll().slice(-5);
  parts.push(`Recent deals: ${JSON.stringify(ledger)}`);
  
  // Top operators
  const ops = operatorProfiles().getAll().slice(0, 10);
  parts.push(`Operator profiles: ${JSON.stringify(ops)}`);
  
  return parts.join('\n\n');
}
```

This is the ContextFactory pattern applied to chat — pre-computed, scoped context objects, not raw database dumps.

## Constraints
- Use safeLlmCall with expectedMaxOutput: 1024
- Token meter the chat calls separately (capability: "chat")
- 628 backend tests must still pass
- Don't overcomplicate — this is a text input and a response display, not a multi-turn agent loop. Multi-turn comes later.
```

This gives you a direct line to your intelligence layer from Day 1. When you're on the phone with Priester and need to know "what did we pay for midsize KTEB-KMIA last time?" — you ask Dumont in the chat instead of digging through tables.

# Dumont Chat — AI Co-Pilot in Mission Control

Read existing files before creating anything. 628 tests must still pass.

## Backend

### 1. Create src/server/chat-context.ts

Build a token-optimized context injector. NOT raw JSON.stringify — human-readable, dense text format:

```typescript
export function buildChatContext(dealId?: string): string
```

Assembles context from real SQLite stores (DealStore, OperatorProfileStore, ValidationLedgerStore). Four sections:

- ACTIVE PIPELINE: count of deals by stage (one line)
- CURRENT DEAL FOCUS (if dealId): route, pax, estimate range, operator, OSA price, stage, guardian status (5-8 lines max)
- RECENT COMPLETED DEALS: last 5 ValidationLedger entries, one line each: `[date] route: Op $X → OSA $Y (Margin Z%). Outcome: status`
- TOP OPERATORS: top 5 by reliability score, one line each: `Name (Base): Reliability X, Speed Ym, Delta +Z%`

Total context must stay under 500 tokens. This is the ContextFactory pattern — compass, not encyclopedia.

### 2. Create src/server/routes/chat.ts

SSE streaming endpoint. Do NOT use safeLlmCall — it waits for full response. Use Anthropic SDK streaming directly, but manually meter tokens.

```typescript
chatRouter.post("/api/chat", authMiddleware, async (req, res) => {
  // Validate { message: string, dealId?: string }
  // Build system prompt from BASE_PROMPT + buildChatContext(dealId)
  // Estimate input tokens and log
  // Set SSE headers (Content-Type: text/event-stream, Cache-Control: no-cache)
  // Stream via client.messages.stream()
  // On each text chunk: res.write(`data: ${JSON.stringify({ text })}\n\n`)
  // On end: res.write("data: [DONE]\n\n"), log output tokens, res.end()
  // On error: log, send error event, end
})
```

System prompt:
"You are Dumont, the AI deal engine for Orange Sunshine Aviation. You are talking to Phelipe, the founder and ATP-rated pilot-in-command. You have access to the current deal pipeline, operator intelligence, and pricing data. Answer questions about deals, operators, routes, and pricing using the data provided. Be direct, use numbers, no filler. If a margin looks compressed, flag it. If an operator's response time is degrading, mention it."

Use claude-sonnet-4-20250514 (Sonnet for speed on conversational queries, not Opus).
max_tokens: 1024.

### 3. Register in server/index.ts

Import chatRouter, app.use(chatRouter).

## Frontend

### 4. Create dashboard/src/components/ChatView.tsx

Terminal-aesthetic chat, NOT a consumer chatbot bubble UI.

- Header: "DUMONT AI" in OSA orange, monospaced. If a deal is active, show "CTX: {dealId}" in muted text.
- Message list: scrollable. User messages labeled "PIC" (pilot in command), AI messages labeled "DUMONT".

- Input: single-line text input at bottom, placeholder "Query intelligence layer...", auto-focus.
- No markdown rendering for v1 — raw monospaced text is correct for a terminal tool.

Fetch from the API using SSE:
- POST /api/chat with Bearer token auth
- Read the stream with ReadableStream reader
- Parse SSE data chunks, append text to the last message
- On [DONE], stop streaming indicator

- Add "Dumont" tab after Autonomy (keyboard shortcut: 7)
- Pass activeDealId (the currently selected deal in Pipeline) to ChatView
- Command bar: /chat [message] sends a message to Dumont without switching tabs

## Design Rules

- Monospaced font throughout the chat

The `./data/` directory doesn't exist on Railway. Need to auto-create it.The `./data/` directory doesn't exist on Railway's container. Quick fix — make `getDb()` create it automatically:

```
# Fix: Auto-create data directory in database.ts

In src/memory/database.ts, add this BEFORE the new Database() call:

import { mkdirSync } from "node:fs";
import { dirname } from "node:path";

// Inside getDb(), before creating the Database instance:
mkdirSync(dirname(dbPath), { recursive: true });
```

Run that in Claude Code, commit, push. Railway will redeploy and the crash stops.

Also: set up a **Railway Volume Mount** on `/app/data` so the database file persists across deploys. Without it, every deploy creates a fresh empty database.

## Claude

The user wants me to give my design opinion on Gemini's spec, then build a Claude Code prompt that merges the best decisions.Gemini's spec is 80% right. Here's where I disagree and why:

**Keep the bottom command bar. Don't replace with Cmd+K.**

Gemini says cut it. Wrong. The command bar is your most differentiated UI element — it's what makes Mission Control feel like a cockpit, not another SaaS dashboard. Linear's Cmd+K works because Linear users already have muscle memory for it. You don't have users to retrain. The command bar is always visible, always reminding you what's possible. It's a ForeFlight approach (instruments always visible) vs a Linear approach (hidden until summoned). For a solo founder managing 3-5 deals, always-visible wins.

**Keep Dumont as a full tab, not a side panel.**

Gemini says 400px sliding drawer. Wrong for your use case. When you're talking to Dumont about deal strategy, you want full-width attention on the conversation, not a cramped sidebar competing with the deal detail. The tab approach is correct. What you should add: when you're on the Pipeline tab and hit Cmd+\, it opens Dumont with the selected deal's context pre-loaded. Best of both worlds.

**Keep the SDR kanban.**

Gemini says convert to a list. Disagree. The kanban gives you instant visual distribution of lead quality — you can see "3 qualified, 1 no budget, 2 not qualified" at a glance without reading numbers. Lists require scanning. The kanban is already working. Polish it, don't replace it.

**Agree on everything else:** 12 color tokens, 4px border radius only, 2 fonts (Inter + JetBrains Mono), the deal card density spec, the 3-column detail layout, the pricing waterfall, the approve/reject inline flow, cutting dead components, and the keyboard shortcuts.

## Phase 1: Fix Critical Bugs (do these first, verify after each)

### 1A. Wire keyboard shortcuts (the worst audit finding)
In App.tsx, add a global keydown handler:

```typescript
useEffect(() => {
  const handler = (e: KeyboardEvent) => {
    // Don't capture when typing in input/textarea
    if (e.target instanceof HTMLInputElement || e.target instanceof HTMLTextAreaElement) return;
    
    // Tab switching: 1-7
    const tabs = ["pipeline", "inbox", "calls", "sdr", "autonomy", "intelligence", "dumont"];
    if (e.key >= "1" && e.key <= "7" && !e.metaKey && !e.ctrlKey) {
      setActiveTab(tabs[parseInt(e.key) - 1]);
      e.preventDefault();
    }
    
    // / to focus command bar
    if (e.key === "/" && !e.metaKey) {
      document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>('[data-command-input]')?.focus();
      e.preventDefault();
    }
    
    // Escape to deselect deal
    if (e.key === "Escape") {
      setSelectedDealId(null);
      e.preventDefault();
    }
    
    // Cmd+\ to switch to Dumont tab
    if (e.key === "\\" && (e.metaKey || e.ctrlKey)) {
      setActiveTab("dumont");
      e.preventDefault();
    }
  };
  
  window.addEventListener("keydown", handler);
  return () => window.removeEventListener("keydown", handler);
}, []);
```

3. **Operator settlement patterns** — which operators need money fastest (they're cash-strapped, give them early pay for 0.5% discount), which ones are fine with weekly settlement.

**Tech Stack for the Map:**

- **Deck.gl** (Uber's open-source map framework) — built for millions of data points, WebGL rendered, handles ADS-B track lines natively. Or **Mapbox GL JS** for a simpler start.
- **ADS-B data source**: ADSBexchange API ($10/mo for full feed) or OpenSky Network (free, 5-second delay)
- **Backend**: new ADS-B ingestion worker that polls every 30 seconds, stores positions in SQLite (or TimescaleDB at scale), builds the origin-destination matrix nightly
- **Historical storage**: 90 days of positions = ~50-100GB compressed. Store in S3/R2, query on demand for replay

**What to Build When:**

| Phase | What | Why |
|-------|------|-----|
| Now | Nothing. Ship Deal 1 first. | The map doesn't close deals. |
| After Deal 5 | ADS-B ingestion for YOUR operators only (5-10 tails) | Prove ghost positioning on real deals |
| After Deal 15 | Radar view in MC with live positions | Operational tool for you |
| Before YC interview | Historical replay + backtest | The $2.4M ghost spread number for the pitch |
| Post-YC | Full Part 135 fleet tracking (12K+ tails) | The market intelligence platform |

**The honest sequencing:** The map is the most visually impressive thing you could build. YC partners would lose their minds seeing live aircraft on a Bloomberg-style terminal. But it doesn't close Deal 1. Build the Mercury payment flow and close deals first. The map earns its place when you have operator relationships and need to prove the ghost positioning thesis with real data.

When you're ready, the Radar view is one React component + one ADS-B ingestion worker + one new SQLite table. The architecture supports it today.

## Claude

The user wants a prompt for Gemini to audit and improve the Radar/live map concept.```
I'm building Mission Control — the internal operations dashboard for a private aviation charter brokerage. We've already built and deployed: deal pipeline, inbox, calls, SDR kanban, autonomy tracking, intelligence (ValidationLedger + KPIs), and a Dumont AI chat co-pilot.

Now I'm designing the next major feature: a live ADS-B radar view that tracks aircraft positions, enables historical replay, ghost positioning detection, and AI-powered simulation. Think Bloomberg Terminal meets FlightAware meets a trading floor's risk dashboard — but for charter aviation market-making.

I need you to audit this architecture hard, find the gaps, improve the design, and challenge every assumption. Be brutal.

## The Business Context

OSA is a zero-commission AI-powered charter brokerage. We own zero aircraft. Our moat is information asymmetry:

1. **Ghost Positioning Spread** — the charter market wastes $800M-1.2B annually in unnecessary positioning legs because no broker has fleet-wide visibility. When Operator X quotes a $35K trip assuming a 40-minute deadhead from Denver, but our ADS-B data shows Operator Y's aircraft is already sitting at the origin airport, we eliminate the phantom deadhead. We capture the spread as margin. Estimated 15-25% of all charter flights have a ghost positioning opportunity.

2. **Operator Signal Ratio** — legacy brokers spam 40 RFQs and get 4 quotes (2.5% signal). We send 3 targeted RFQs based on physics validation and get 3 quotes (33% signal). The radar view is what enables this targeting.

3. **Route Liquidity Index (RLI)** — time-aware supply density. RLI(airport, lead_time) = available_tails_within(positioning_radius(lead_time)) / baseline_demand(airport, day_of_week). Dynamic margin optimization: 8% on liquid routes, 18% on constrained.

4. **The Data Lake** — every ADS-B position, every deal, every operator quote builds a transaction intelligence dataset that doesn't exist elsewhere. At 10,000 transactions this becomes a proprietary foundation for charter market intelligence.

## What I've Designed So Far

### Radar View (new Mission Control tab)

**Live Map:**
- Full-screen map showing real-time Part 135 aircraft positions from ADS-B
- Color-coded: airborne (blue), ground/available (green), ground idle 12h+ (amber)
- Click aircraft: tail, operator, type, home base, last 5 routes, estimated availability
- Active deals overlaid as route arcs with matched operator aircraft highlighted
- Ghost positioning opportunities highlighted (aircraft at origin that could eliminate a deadhead)

**Historical Replay:**
- Timeline scrubber to replay any day in past 90 days
- Watch fleet movements, validate ghost positioning after the fact
- Build origin-destination matrix visually
- Spot seasonal patterns (Palm Beach corridor Nov-Apr, Aspen Dec-Mar + Jul)

**Dumont Analysis Layer:**
- Natural language queries on the map: "What's available midsize within 60nm of KTEB?"
- Ghost spread calculation on demand: "Ghost spread KTEB corridor last 30 days?"
- Operator utilization queries: "How many hours did Priester's Challenger fleet fly in March?"

**Simulators:**
- Run hypothetical scenarios on historical data
- "How many ghost positioning opportunities existed on KTEB-KPBI in February?"
- "What if I added Solairus to my network? How does Northeast coverage change?"
- "Simulate Super Bowl weekend — what happens to RLI on KTEB-KLAS?"

### Proposed Tech Stack
- Deck.gl or Mapbox GL JS for WebGL map rendering
- ADSBexchange API ($10/mo) or OpenSky Network (free, 5-second delay)
- ADS-B ingestion worker polling every 30 seconds
- SQLite for positions (or TimescaleDB at scale)
- 90 days historical = ~50-100GB compressed, stored in S3/R2
- React component in existing Mission Control dashboard

### Proposed Phasing
- Phase 0 (now): Don't build it. Close Deal 1 first.
- Phase 1 (after 5 deals): ADS-B ingestion for operator network only (5-10 tails)
- Phase 2 (after 15 deals): Radar view in Mission Control
- Phase 3 (before YC): Historical replay + ghost spread backtest
- Phase 4 (post-YC): Full Part 135 fleet tracking (12K+ tails)

## What I Need From You

### 1. Architecture Audit

Tear apart the technical architecture:
- Is Deck.gl the right choice or is there something better for this use case? Consider Cesium, Kepler.gl, or pure Mapbox.
- SQLite for time-series position data — does this break at 12K tails × 30-second updates × 90 days? What's the actual storage math? When does it need to migrate to TimescaleDB or ClickHouse?
- The ingestion worker polling every 30 seconds — is this the right architecture or should it be WebSocket streaming from ADSBexchange?
- How do you efficiently query "all aircraft of type X within radius Y of airport Z that have been idle for more than T hours" on 90 days of position data? What indexes matter?

### 2. Ghost Positioning Detection Algorithm

Design the actual algorithm, not hand-waving:
- Given a trip request (origin, destination, aircraft class, date), how do you identify ghost positioning opportunities?
- What's the false positive rate? An aircraft on the ground at KASE might be there for maintenance, owner use, or another booking — how do you filter?
- How do you calculate the dollar value of a ghost positioning capture? What's the formula?
- For the backtest: given 500 historical ADS-B flights, write pseudocode for detecting every ghost positioning event and calculating total market waste.

### 3. RLI Calculation Engine

The Route Liquidity Index needs to be real, not theoretical:
- How do you define "available" from ADS-B data alone? Idle 12h+ is a heuristic, not a fact.
- How do you handle the time-aware positioning radius expansion (6 hours = 500nm, 72 hours = nationwide)?
- What's the baseline demand denominator? Historical departures from that airport on that day of week? How much historical data do you need for statistical significance?
- Can RLI be calculated in real-time for a live deal, or does it need to be pre-computed?

### 4. Data Architecture for the Transaction Intelligence Layer

The ADS-B data combined with deal data creates the proprietary dataset. Design the schema:
- What's the optimal data model for position data (time-series vs event-sourced vs append-only log)?
- How do you join ADS-B positions with deal records efficiently?
- What aggregations should be pre-computed nightly vs computed on demand?
- At what scale does this need its own database separate from the deal engine SQLite?

### 5. The Simulation Engine

I want to run "what-if" scenarios on historical data:
- "What if OSA had been brokering on the KTEB-KPBI corridor in February? How many ghost opportunities, what total spread?"
- "What if I add 3 new operators in the Southeast? How does my coverage map change?"
- "Simulate a demand spike on KTEB-KLAS — at what point does RLI drop below 1.0 and margin should increase?"

Design the simulation architecture:
- What data does each simulation type need?
- How long should a simulation take to run? (Target: under 10 seconds for a 30-day replay)
- Can Dumont trigger simulations via natural language, or does it need a structured query interface?

### 6. Competitive Intelligence

Who else is doing anything like this? Specifically:
- Does any existing charter broker have ADS-B-powered positioning?
- Does Tuvoli/Directional Aviation track fleet positions across their portfolio?
- Has anyone built a ghost positioning detection system in any aviation vertical (commercial, cargo, charter)?
- Are there academic papers on positioning optimization in charter or fractional aviation?

### 7. What I'm Missing

What haven't I thought of? Specific gaps:
- Regulatory or legal risks of using ADS-B data commercially for pricing decisions?
- LADD (FAA block list) compliance — can I track aircraft whose operators have requested privacy?
- ADS-B data quality issues — what percentage of Part 135 aircraft have reliable ADS-B out?
- Edge cases that break the ghost positioning thesis (aircraft maintenance, owner trips, crew duty limits)

### 8. The YC Demo

If I have 5 minutes to show this to a YC partner, what's the exact demo flow?
- What do I show first?
- What's the "holy shit" moment?
- How do I connect the live map to revenue and margin?
- What question will they ask, and what's my answer?

Be specific. Give me implementable architecture, not concepts. I want to hand this to a coding assistant and have it build the ADS-B ingestion layer, the ghost positioning detector, and the map visualization.
```

The user is asking about who would be the authority/reference for building the benchmark and intelligence systems for an AI-native charter broker. They want to know which companies, people, or frameworks would be the best references for building these specific competitive intelligence and market-making systems.The authorities aren't in aviation. Nobody in aviation has built what you're describing. The references come from industries that already solved the same information asymmetry problem:

**Tier 1 — The Direct Analogs (they built exactly this in different markets)**

- **Citadel Securities / Ken Griffin** — market-making with information asymmetry. They don't trade on opinion, they trade on seeing the order flow before anyone else. Your ghost positioning spread IS their bid-ask spread. They built the infrastructure to see the entire market in real-time and capture the spread between participants who can't see each other. Study how they think about latency, data ingestion, and position management.

- **Flexport / Ryan Petersen** — did to freight forwarding what you're doing to charter. Fragmented market with no price transparency, legacy brokers with zero technology, massive information asymmetry between shippers and carriers. Built visibility (live tracking), pricing intelligence (rate benchmarking), and became the system of record. $8B valuation. Your ADS-B radar IS their container tracking. Your ValidationLedger IS their rate benchmarking database.

- **Orbital Insight / James Crawford** — satellite imagery + AI to predict economic activity. They count cars in Walmart parking lots to predict quarterly earnings. You're counting aircraft at FBOs to predict operator utilization and route demand. Same pattern: alternative data source + computation = intelligence nobody else has.

**Tier 2 — The Pattern References (they solved the specific sub-problems)**

- **Kensho / Daniel Nadler** (acquired by S&P Global for $550M) — built AI analytics on financial data that humans couldn't process fast enough. His framework: "What would a team of 50 analysts produce if they worked 24/7 with perfect memory?" That's Dumont analyzing your ADS-B data lake. The benchmark suite you're designing is Kensho's analytical engine applied to aviation.

- **Palantir / Alex Karp** — the knowledge graph authority. Their entire product is connecting data sources that don't talk to each other and making them queryable. Your Layer 0 (FAA data + ADS-B + operator profiles + deal history) IS a Palantir-style knowledge graph for a single vertical. Study Gotham's entity resolution and relationship mapping.

- **Uber's Marketplace Team / Dawn Chen** — dynamic pricing based on real-time supply/demand. Your RLI is their surge pricing. They built the exact same two-dimensional surface: available_drivers_within(radius) / current_demand. The time-aware expansion (6 hours = 500nm, 72 hours = nationwide) mirrors how Uber's radius expands during low-demand periods. Study their engineering blog posts on geospatial indexing and supply prediction.

**Tier 3 — The Visualization and Interface References**

- **Mapbox / Eric Gundersen** — if you're building the radar view, Mapbox is the authority on real-time geospatial visualization at scale. Their case studies with Uber, Instacart, and the NYT show how to render millions of data points without killing the browser.

- **Observable / Mike Bostock** (creator of D3.js) — the authority on making data explorable. Your simulator / backtest replay needs to feel interactive, not like watching a recording. Bostock's philosophy: the user should be able to ask questions of the data by manipulating the visualization directly.

- **Numerai / Richard Craib** — built a hedge fund where the data IS the moat. Their tournament structure (give data to thousands of models, measure who predicts best) is conceptually what you're doing with your pricing engine: measure physics estimate vs actual quote, narrow the delta, compound the accuracy.

**The Framework to Steal:**

From Citadel: **"See the entire board. Everyone else sees their own pieces."** That's your one-sentence description of the ADS-B radar.

From Flexport: **"Digitize the transaction, own the data, become the infrastructure."** That's your sequencing from broker → payment rail → intelligence platform.

From Orbital Insight: **"Alternative data + domain expertise = alpha."** ADS-B is your alternative data. Your ATP certificate is your domain expertise. The combination is your alpha.

From Kensho: **"Benchmark everything. If you can't measure it, you can't compound it."** That's why the 7 benchmarks matter — they're not vanity metrics, they're the measurement infrastructure that proves the compounding.

as if Citadel's quant team designed a market-making engine

```typescript
// The full YC-ready ledger row — every closed deal gets one
export const ValidationLedgerEntrySchema = z.object({
  // Existing fields (keep all)
  id: z.string(),
  dealId: z.string(),
  route: z.string(),
  date: z.string(),
  
  // === NEW: The 7 Benchmark Columns ===

  ghostValueCents: z.number().default(0),           // $ saved by eliminating phantom deadhead (integer cents)
  ghostDescription: z.string().optional(),           // e.g., "N345XA already at KASE, eliminated KAPA positioning"
  
  // Benchmark 2: Operator Signal Ratio
  rfqsSent: z.number().default(0),                   // how many RFQs sent for this deal
  quotesReceived: z.number().default(0),             // how many quotes came back
  
  // Benchmark 3: Route Liquidity Index
  rli: z.enum(["high", "medium", "low"]).optional(), // supply density at time of quote
  rliScore: z.number().optional(),                    // raw numeric RLI value
  
  // Benchmark 4: Fleet Resilience
  tripOutcome: z.enum(["completed", "disruption_recovered", "disruption_failed", "cancelled"]).default("completed"),
  recoveryUsed: z.boolean().default(false),           // did we need to swap aircraft?
  recoveryTimeMin: z.number().optional(),             // minutes to source replacement if recovery used
  
  // Benchmark 5: Demand Prediction (filled async from analytics)
  routePageViews7d: z.number().optional(),            // route page traffic in the 7 days before this deal
  
  // Benchmark 6: Client Decision Velocity
  optionsPresentedAt: z.string().optional(),          // ISO timestamp when client saw options
  clientConfirmedAt: z.string().optional(),           // ISO timestamp when client committed
  decisionVelocityMin: z.number().optional(),         // computed: minutes between presented and confirmed
  
  // Benchmark 7: Network Density (snapshot at time of deal)
  operatorsInNetwork: z.number().optional(),
  operatorsInMetro: z.number().optional(),            // operators within 100nm of departure
  
  // === Timing ===
  leadTimeHours: z.number().optional(),               // hours from request to departure
  
  // === Pricing Engine Accuracy ===
  physicsEstimateCents: z.number().optional(),        // what our engine predicted (integer cents)
  operatorQuoteCents: z.number().optional(),          // what the operator actually quoted
  osaClientPriceCents: z.number().optional(),         // what we charged the client
  marginPercent: z.number().optional(),               // realized margin
  estimateDeltaPercent: z.number().optional(),        // (operatorQuote - physicsEstimate) / physicsEstimate * 100
  
  // === Operator Intelligence ===
  operatorName: z.string().optional(),
  operatorBase: z.string().optional(),
  operatorResponseMin: z.number().optional(),         // minutes from RFQ sent to quote received
  operatorReliabilityScore: z.number().optional(),    // score at time of deal
  
  // === Outcome ===
  outcome: z.enum(["booked", "lost_price", "lost_timing", "lost_ghosted", "lost_other", "cancelled"]).optional(),
  revenueCents: z.number().optional(),
  notes: z.string().optional(),
  
  // === Payment State (Mercury flow) ===
  paymentStatus: z.enum([
    "pending",           // deal closed, no invoice yet
    "invoiced",          // payment instructions sent to client
    "client_paid",       // Mercury webhook: wire/ACH received
    "operator_paid",     // Mercury API: outbound wire sent
    "margin_captured"    // operator confirmed, margin is ours
  ]).default("pending"),
  clientPaidAt: z.string().optional(),
  operatorPaidAt: z.string().optional(),
  floatWindowHours: z.number().optional(),            // hours between client_paid and operator_paid
  
  createdAt: z.string(),
  updatedAt: z.string(),
});
